_readme: WHO THEY ARE FOR: children who find the textbook hard. The owner asked for
them to sit a little BELOW textbook level on purpose. The rule used here is:
structures from the grade below, vocabulary at grade level, with the pictures
carrying the new words so the child is never stuck mid-sentence.
Levels were taken from data/games/grade-3..6.json, which records the units and
outcomes of the Sri Lankan Pupil's Books. Grade 6 is marked 'awaiting-source'
there and has only grammar topics, so the Grade 6 stories follow those topics
and the natural step up from Grade 5 rather than named units.
AGE, NOT ABILITY: a Grade 6 pupil reading below level must not be handed
something babyish. The language gets simpler down the grades; the situations
stay age-appropriate - the market, a cricket match, the last bus home.
PICTURES: write {word} in a line and the build swaps in
assets/img/games/<word>.svg, the Game Zone drawings - about 550 bytes each.
Only words that have a drawing may be used; the build warns if one is missing.
Run: ls assets/img/games to see what exists.

pages.title: Picture Readers
pages.metaTitle: Free Picture Readers for Sri Lankan Children, Grades 3 to 6 | RCF English
pages.description: Twenty free rebus stories for Grades 3 to 6, where pictures stand in for words. Written below textbook level for children who find English reading hard.
pages.keywords: rebus stories, picture readers, easy English reading Sri Lanka, graded readers for children

hero.text: Stories where a picture stands in for a word. The child reads the sentence and says the word aloud - which is how the word is remembered.

blocks.heading: Who these are for
text: These are for the child who can decode English words but reads so slowly that the meaning is lost by the end of the sentence. Every teacher knows the one: careful, willing, and three pages behind.

The language here sits **a little below** the textbook for the grade on purpose. A reader is not a lesson. Its job is to be finished, and to be finished comfortably, because a child who completes a whole story in English thinks something different about themselves afterwards.

What makes a rebus story work is that the child is never stranded. When an unfamiliar word arrives it is a picture, so the sentence keeps moving. The word is learned in the middle of a story rather than in a list.

blocks.heading: How to use one
intro: Ten minutes is enough. These are not a lesson and should not become one.

items.title: Let the child read it aloud, pictures and all
text: When they reach a picture they say the word. If they do not know it, tell them at once and move on - do not make them guess at length, which is the fastest way to turn reading into a test.

items.title: Read it a second time
text: The second reading is where fluency comes from. It will be noticeably faster than the first, and the child will hear the difference themselves.

items.title: Then press Show the words
text: The pictures turn into the written words. Read it once more. The child has now met each new word in a sentence they already understand, which is the whole point.

items.title: Talk about it
text: Each story has two or three questions at the end. Ask them in English if the child can manage, in the first language if not. Understanding the story matters more than answering in English.

blocks.heading: Choose a grade
intro: Five stories in each. If a child struggles with their own grade, drop down one - nothing here says which grade it is on the page itself.

items.title: Grade 3
text: Three to six words a sentence. *This is my… It is… I like…* My ball, my garden, my school bag, the market, my family.

items.title: Grade 4
text: *There is… There are…* and *I am going…* A rainy day, helping father, the bus to school, our classroom, the kite.

items.title: Grade 5
text: The past tense arrives. The dry well, the temple lamp, the cricket match, the peacock, grandmother's medicine.

items.title: Grade 6
text: Longer sentences and some conversation. The last bus, the tailor's shop, saving the pond, the solar lamp, the postman.

blocks.title: For teachers: why the pictures are not decoration
text: A picture in place of a word does something a picture beside the text cannot. It sits in the grammar of the sentence, so the child has to work out what kind of word belongs there before they name it - and that is reading, not guessing from a picture.
It also keeps the sentence moving. A second-language reader who stops at an unknown word usually loses the whole sentence; here there is nothing to stop at.

pages.title: Picture Readers: Grade 5
pages.metaTitle: Five Easy Picture Stories for Grade 5 English | RCF English
pages.description: Five free rebus stories for Grade 5: The Dry Well, The Temple Lamp, The Cricket Match, The Peacock and Grandmother's Medicine. Written in the past tense.
pages.keywords: Grade 5 English reading, easy stories for children, rebus story, past tense reading

hero.text: Five stories, all of them about something that already happened.

stories.title: 1. The Dry Well
lines: Last year there was no {rain} for many weeks.
The {well} in our garden was almost dry.
My {father} took a {bucket} and went to the {well}.
There was only a little {water} at the bottom.
We used it carefully for the {flower} plants.
Then one evening a big black {cloud} came over the hills.
In the morning the {well} was full again.
questions: Why was the well nearly dry?
What did they use the last water for?

stories.title: 2. The Temple Lamp
lines: On Poya day my {grandmother} took me to the {temple}.
She carried a white {flower} in her hand.
An old man gave us a {cup} of {tea}.
My {grandmother} lit the {oil-lamp} and closed her {eyes}.
We walked home when the {moon} came up.
questions: What did each of them carry?

stories.title: 3. The Cricket Match
lines: Our school had a {cricket} match on Saturday.
We needed four runs to win.
I hit it as hard as I could.
All my friends were shouting my name.
Our {teacher} gave me a {book} as a prize.
questions: How many runs did they need?

stories.title: 4. The Peacock
lines: Early one morning I went to the {paddyfield} with my {uncle}.
Suddenly we saw a {peacock} near the water.
Its long {feather}s were blue and green.
Then a {crow} made a loud noise.
The {peacock} opened its tail and ran into the trees.
My {uncle} said it was good luck to see one.
questions: Where did they go, and when?

stories.title: 5. Grandmother's Medicine
lines: My {grandmother} was not well last week.
My {mother} took her to the {hospital} by {bus}.
A {doctor} looked at her for a long time.
After three days she was much better.
She made {sweets} for all of us.
questions: How did they go to the hospital?
How do we know she got better?

pages.title: Picture Readers: Grade 6
pages.metaTitle: Five Easy Picture Stories for Grade 6 English | RCF English
pages.description: Five free rebus stories for Grade 6: The Last Bus, The Tailor's Shop, Saving the Pond, The Solar Lamp and The Postman. Longer sentences with some conversation.
pages.keywords: Grade 6 English reading, easy stories, rebus story, reading practice Sri Lanka

hero.text: Five stories with longer sentences and some conversation.

stories.title: 1. The Last Bus
lines: It was raining hard when school finished. {rain}
I waited at the {bus-stop} with my friend Kamal.
The {clock} on the shop wall showed half past five.
"The last {bus} comes at six," Kamal said.
We stood under one {umbrella} and watched the water run down the road.
A {van} went past and splashed us both.
At last the {bus} came, and it was almost empty.
We sat near the {window} and talked all the way home.
questions: What time did the last bus come?
Why did they get wet twice?
How do you know they were not in a hurry at the end?

stories.title: 2. The Tailor's Shop
lines: My {mother} took my old {shirt} to the {tailor} near the {market}.
His shop was small and there was cloth on every {table}.
"Can you make this bigger?" my {mother} asked him.
The {tailor} looked at the {shirt} and smiled.
"He is growing too fast," he said.
I stood in front of the {mirror} while he measured my arms.
My {mother} gave him a {banknote} and we walked home.
On Friday the {shirt} fitted me perfectly.
questions: Why did they go to the tailor?
How long did the work take?

stories.title: 3. Saving the Pond
lines: There is a small {pond} behind our {school}.
Last term the {water} was dirty and there were no {fish} in it.
People threw things in instead of using the {dustbin}.
Our class decided to clean it.
We worked there every Friday afternoon for a month.
Then we put up a board beside it. {recycle}
By November the {water} was clear again.
Last week somebody saw a small {fish}.
questions: How long did the class work?
What is the last sentence telling us?

stories.title: 4. The Solar Lamp
lines: Our village had no electricity until last year.
I used to do my homework beside an {oil-lamp}.
The light was weak and my {eyes} hurt after an hour.
Then men came and put a {solar-panel} on our {roof}.
Now one {bulb} burns in every room after dark.
My {father} says the {sun} works for us all day and asks for nothing.
I can read my {book} until nine o'clock.
My marks are better this term.
questions: What did father mean about the sun?

stories.title: 5. The Postman
lines: Every morning at ten the {postman} comes down our lane on his {bicycle}.
His bag is always full and he never stops to rest.
Last Monday he brought a letter for my {sister}.
It was from the university in Colombo.
She read it twice and then she began to cry.
My {mother} ran to the {temple} with a {flower}.
My {father} went to the {market} and bought {sweets} for the whole lane.
questions: What does the last sentence tell us about the family?
